item.title: Giving Thanks After a Bumpy Year in Markets
item.dc:creator: Morgan Stanley
item.description: Morgan Stanley · Thoughts on the Market — This Thanksgiving weekend, our Global Head of Fixed Income Research Andrew Sheets talks about the origins of the holiday, what investors should be grateful for and the outlook for the year ahead. Read more insights from Morgan Stanley. ----- Transcript ----- Andrew Sheets: Welcome to Thoughts on the Market. I'm Andrew Sheets, Global Head of Fixed Income Research at Morgan Stanley. Today, giving thanks. It's Friday, November 27th at 2pm in London. Thanksgiving has always been one of my favorite holidays. A jolly mix of turkey, football, overeating, and napping. The lighthearted nature of the holiday, the fact that it's really about food and family and friends is, for me, a deep part of the appeal. But amidst the stuffing, the pie, and a Lions game, it's easy to forget that Thanksgiving was born out of much more serious stuff. The Pilgrims initially set out on two ships, the Mayflower and the Speedwell. But the Speedwell started leaking. They had to turn back not once, but twice; eventually abandoning this lesser-known ship and crowding into the more famous Mayflower. This delay was pretty unfortunate. It meant that they were now crossing the North Atlantic late in the season with…

item.title: Rates reflect resilient growth, not high deficits. Inflation risks two-sided
item.dc:creator: Bank of America
item.description: Bank of America · Global Research Unlocked — Real yields reflect resilience; supply shocks remain a risk Mark Cabana argues that fiscal concerns have played only a limited role in the increase in Treasury yields over the last year, with resilient US growth accounting for most of the upside in real rates. He discusses what we'd need to see in order for a debt spiral to become a reasonable risk and what would need to change for yields to move sustainably lower. He also shares his view on why risks around the Fed may still be skewed toward more tightening than markets currently price. Looking into 2027, consensus expects inflation to moderate as oil and other supply shocks fade, but Mark sees the distribution of outcomes for inflation as two sided. With much of the benign inflation outlook already reflected in markets, he discusses the risk that renewed commodity or supply pressures could keep rates higher for longer. item.title: Can Treasuries Still Protect Your Portfolio?
item.dc:creator: Morgan Stanley
item.description: Morgan Stanley · Thoughts on the Market — When stocks fall, investors often turn to government bonds. Our Global Head of Macro Strategy Matthew Hornbach looks at whether the market's favorite hedge has lost its appeal. Read more insights from Morgan Stanley. ----- Transcript ----- Matthew Hornbach: Welcome to Thoughts on the Market. I'm Matthew Hornbach, Global Head of Macro Strategy at Morgan Stanley. Today, can Treasuries once again protect a portfolio when stocks fall? It's Tuesday, November 24th at 10am in New York. Last week, the S&P 500 fell every day and closed in correction territory. Doubts about the AI trade drove most of the selling, and Treasuries rallied even as Fed officials argued for more rate hikes. Ten-year yields fell about a fifth of a percentage point on the week back below 5 percent. That's what a hedge is supposed to do. For much of the past few years, however, Treasuries fell alongside stocks instead. In our view, Treasuries can work as a hedge again when the worry is about slower growth. When the worry is about inflation, however, bonds and stocks still tend to fall together. It ultimately comes down to what investors expect the Fed to do next. When inflation is the problem, the Fed raises rates.…

item.title: What Will Determine the Durability of the AI Investment Cycle?
item.dc:creator: Goldman Sachs
item.description: Goldman Sachs · Goldman Sachs Exchanges — Will AI-related market stresses and regulatory uncertainty stall investment in AI? Demand, capital, and power supply may determine whether the investment cycle endures, Social Capital CEO Chamath Palihapitiya and Eric Sheridan of Goldman Sachs Research say on the Exchanges podcast. Key takeaways: Returns on AI investment remain elusive: Implementation and change management are hurdles to adoption and productivity gains, Palihapitiya says. Large companies are not yet seeing return on investment that shows up in earnings. Neoclouds need end-customers to see meaningful returns on their AI spend: Their revenue is short-term and speculative but must cover long-term, fixed costs, Palihapitiya says, leaving neoclouds dependent on the utilization rates of the data center capacity they’ve committed to deliver. Demand from large customers and steady AI usage will be critical. The investment cycle can still deliver attractive returns: Sheridan’s analysis suggests the major US hyperscalers can “very easily” earn returns of at least 15% on their investment, backed by their contracted future revenue and strong core businesses. Demand, capital, and power will be key for sustaining the AI…

item.title: Must Read Research: Are Pack Rips Gaming’s Next Big Thing?
item.dc:creator: Bank of America
item.description: Bank of America · Global Research Unlocked — The traditional thrill of opening a pack of trading cards is going digital, and the numbers are hard to ignore. In this special episode of Must Read Research on BofA Global Research Unlocked, Head of Global Research, Candace Browning sits down with Gaming Analyst Julie Hoover to explore the rise of “pack rips,” where weekly users have surged from roughly 50,000 to more than 1.7 million in just one year. With the category already generating an estimated $2 billion in annualized revenue and a potential market of $30 billion or more, they discuss why the mechanics increasingly resemble online gaming, why operators are moving in, and whether access to rare cards and growing regulatory scrutiny could determine just how big this emerging market becomes. item.title: 2026: The Year Credit Markets Rewired
item.dc:creator: Apollo
item.description: Apollo · Apollo Insights & Outlook (web) — Nearly every investing conversation in 2026 came back to AI, and the borrowing behind it has changed how credit investors look for opportunity. In our latest episode on the convergence of public and private credit markets, Apollo Partners Brian Weinstein and John Cortese discuss how AI accelerated that convergence in 2026, why the barriers between the two markets are expected to continue to erode in 2027, and why credit investors may need to look across the full credit spectrum to find the best opportunities.
